title: DfE Decoded #158: Misogyny Isn't Just an RSHE Issue
author: Paul Urry
summary: Paul Urry responds to the government's new framework for schools to tackle misogyny, prompted by the finding that half of girls heard misogynistic comments in a single week. He argues the key phrase is whole-school approach, because the issue is what children hear in corridors and group chats and what adults challenge, not another RSHE lesson. He explains how algorithms bring harmful content to children without their searching for it, and why calling something banter does not make it harmless. He insists boys must be part of the solution and need a positive account of masculinity, not just warnings, and that staff need confidence rather than scripts. He also stresses listening to girls, bringing parents in, and treating low reporting as a possible sign of low trust. He concludes that culture is what a school allows as well as teaches, and that no national framework can create it for a school.
points: Urry argues that misogyny is a school culture issue, shaped by what adults challenge or ignore, and not something a single RSHE unit can fix.
Ignoring a comment as banter teaches the speaker that the boundary is negotiable and teaches the target that reporting is pointless.
He warns against a strategy that casts boys as the problem, and says schools should help them explore what a good man looks like, including confidence without dominance.
Staff training should build professional judgment for unscripted moments in the dinner queue or on the football pitch, not supply a script for every case.
He cautions against a misogyny action plan or awareness week and urges leaders to check whether existing RSHE, safeguarding, behaviour and pupil voice work join up.
quotes: Half of girls reported hearing misogynistic comments from other pupils during just one week at school.

But ignoring language because it was “only a joke” teaches something too. It teaches the child who said it that the boundary is negotiable. It teaches everyone who heard it what adults are prepared to tolerate.
A strategy for tackling misogyny cannot become a strategy that teaches boys that adults regard them as a problem. That would be counterproductive.
Simply telling boys what not to think leaves a vacuum. Schools can also help them explore something much more positive.
Not giving staff a script for every possible situation. Giving them enough understanding to make good professional judgments when the script doesn’t exist.
Low reporting doesn’t necessarily mean low prevalence. Sometimes it means children don’t believe reporting will change anything.
Because children don’t learn the culture of a school by reading its policies. They learn it from what happens.
But no national framework can create the culture inside an individual school. We do that.
